## First Python notebook

From the extracted `digital-chemistry-course` folder:

```bash
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked marimo edit --headless
```

Open the complete local URL printed in the terminal, then choose `notebooks/00-getting-started.py`. Change an input, follow the dependent cells, and save your own copy.

uv uses `uv.lock` by default. `--locked` stops if it needs updating; without the flag, uv can update it. `--headless` leaves opening the browser to you. In Windows, run the commands in Ubuntu/WSL 2 and use your Windows browser.

[Notebook preview](../notebooks/previews/00-getting-started.html)

## Lecture and MOF practical

We will cover descriptors, training and test splits, overfitting, bias and variance, regularisation, kernels, standardisation, and validation. Worked examples will connect these ideas to the notebook. Our model is closely related to the kernel-ridge models in [Moosavi et al. (2020)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-17755-8); see the [paper example](../lectures/03-mof-uptake.qmd#published-example) for the connection.

Open `notebooks/03-mof-uptake.py` in the same marimo session whenever you are ready:

1. Inspect the descriptors, uptake target, and training/validation/test split.
2. Fit the baseline and compare the unscaled and scaled models. Predict what scaling will change before running them.
3. Record your model choice using validation results, then reveal its test score. Explain what that score tells us about future MOFs.

The [MOF notes and practical instructions](../lectures/03-mof-uptake.qmd#practical) provide the fuller explanation. Stop after the final assessment for today; feature importance and bootstrap uncertainty come later. There is no expectation of finishing everything in class.
